Paul Keating says Defence is trying to 'vandalise the national estate' Opposition is growing to the federal government's plan to sell scores of defence properties to reduce maintenance and repair costs, as locals fight back.

Occupying 15 hectares on the ridgeline of Paddington, the site dates back to the 1840s.

There has been significant pushback to the sale, with several online petitions circulating opposing the plan.

Former prime minister Paul Keating, state Labor MP Marjorie O'Neill and independent Member for Sydney Alex Greenwich are among the vocal critics.

"Victoria Barracks Sydney must remain in the care of the Australian people," Dr O'Neill said.

" Some places are simply too important to sell. "

Sydney's Victoria Barracks in an inner-city precinct surrounded by major stadiums, parks and universities. (ABC News Graphics)

A City of Sydney survey conducted late last year found the main priority for community members was that the heritage of the barracks was maintained.

There was also support for using the site for affordable housing and cultural spaces such museums, galleries, performance areas and artist studios.

The government said it had legal obligations to protect heritage values through the divestment process.

"Departments are engaging with key historical organisations and community groups, including the Australian War Memorial, Shrine of Remembrance, museums and other trusts, to undertake thorough history and heritage planning," a defence spokesperson told the ABC.

Market ready to pounce

The defence estate sales were prompted by a 2023 Defence Strategic Review, which found many large, historic bases were underutilised and a drain on resources.

The audit estimated the department could save upwards of $100 million annually in sustainment costs, but about $1.2 billion would be needed to relocate staff and prepare sites for sale.

The proceeds from the sell-off will be reinvested into the military, with one property developer reportedly offering $5 billion for the entire portfolio.

HMAS Penguin, a Royal Australian Navy base located at Balmoral on the lower north shore of Sydney Harbour in the suburb of Mosman. (Australian Defence Force)

Iain Davidson, state chief executive with Colliers real estate and investment management, said he had already been speaking to potential buyers.

"There is certainly a lot of interest," he told the ABC.

Mr Davidson described the sales as a "one in 50 year" real estate opportunity.

"The portfolio is vast, but a lot of attention is on those prime inner-city barracks sites," he said.

"There's a whole bunch of uses that can come into this … whether it's urban mixed-use precincts, whether it's residential precincts, whether it's seniors living areas."

Sydney's Victoria Barracks is a significant heritage site, housing the Forces Command headquarters and the 2nd Health Brigade. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Defence officials have been quizzed on how much the government expected to make from the individual assets.

Answering a question on notice, they said commercial real estate company Jones Lang LaSalle had undertaken a "desktop market valuation", but disclosing details would "diminish the Commonwealth's commercial advantage when negotiating best market value for each site".

A group of nurses at Victoria Barracks Sydney in 1914. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

The majority of the sites earmarked for sale will eventually be handed over to the Department of Finance, which will be responsible for the tender process to find a buyer.

Mr Davidson said the value would ultimately be set by the market based on the tenderers own "due diligence".

"So that market value will be what that due diligence comes up with and what that highest and best use opportunity is," he said.

" The market's response will be interesting … the market will do the work and let defence know what these assets are worth. "

Victoria Barracks Brisbane, first built in 1864, will be up for sale. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Question of rezoning

The Planning Institute of Australia (PIA) said strategic planning was needed to ensure the sites were repurposed in the public interest.

Government eyes off fire sale of historic defence properties The Albanese government has identified 67 defence sites for potential sale, aiming to unlock up to $1.8 billion.

The organisation is urging the government to "not simply sell to the highest bidder".

Nicole Bennetts, PIA's national head of policy and advocacy, said the organisation recently met with the federal government at a roundtable to discuss best approaches to maximise the sites' long-term national value.

"For us, that's all about actually doing the planning upfront before those sites are divested," Ms Bennetts told the ABC.

"The concern we have is that if you divest them without doing that strategic planning and zoning process, you're putting that master planning process onto the private sector or that future owner, whoever that may be."

The Sydney Waratahs have previously used Victoria Barracks in Sydney's Paddington as a training ground. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

The government has not specified when rezoning could occur.

Mr Davidson believes the government will most likely "leave it to the purchasers to go through the rezoning process".

Community 'none the wiser'

Many community members said they appreciated the government was listening to concerns.

Southbank Residents Association president Tony Penna said it was a "positive" step, but he left the Melbourne event with many unanswered questions.

"To be honest, I was kind of left none the wiser," Mr Penna told the ABC.

"They just said everything we needed to hear. We needed to hear that those heritage spaces will be preserved. We needed to hear that they were going to be accessible to the public.

" But it's still early days. "

Locals hope Melbourne's Victoria Barracks can be used to build a school for the growing population in the area. (ABC News)

Defence said it could take up to two years for complex sites such as Victoria Barracks in Sydney and Melbourne to be ready for sale.

Mr Davidson from Colliers real estate expected other assets could go to market later this year.

Mr Penna, an ADF member who has worked in the barracks, hoped lessons would be learned from the early sales and the community would remain informed.

"Because once a site like Victoria Barracks is sold, it is gone forever," he said.

"Yes, heritage protections exist. Yes, adaptive reuse is promised. But history shows us that once land in prime locations like St Kilda Road enters the private market, commercial pressures inevitably take over."

More than 100 submissions have been made to a Senate inquiry, with a series of public hearings taking place this month.

Defence said additional opportunities for community feedback would continue to arise through the divestment process.

World.title: This island was once ruled by Australia. Now, it could become the world's newest country
World.content:
A tropical archipelago just 1,500 kilometres from Australia, rich in gold and copper, is preparing itself for nationhood next year.

But as Bougainville moves towards independence, unresolved conflicts and memories of a bloody past are coming back to the surface.

Dennis Kuiai joined the Bougainville Revolutionary Army in his early 20s.

Dennis Kuiai says he never wanted to kill anyone.

"But that really is the sort of legacy we are living with now," he says.

"We continue to live with that trauma because we have killed."

Decades after laying down weapons, Dennis Kuiai and other veterans of the Bougainville civil war are still waiting for independence.

In his early 20s, Mr Kuiai was recruited to fight for Bougainville's separatist militia, the Bougainville Revolutionary Army, in a brutal civil war over land, resources and identity.

The conflict claimed up to 15,000 lives.

But while weapons were laid down decades ago, the fight for Bougainville's independence is far from over.

On a humid afternoon, Mr Kuiai shows us around a luscious rainforest landscape that looks like somewhere you might build a luxury resort.

Loading...

Instead, it's slated to become the main prison facility for the prospective nation.

A group of veterans has been employed to prepare the site for construction.

Mr Kuiai says it's a priority project because Bougainville's current prison facilities are extremely limited.

But coming back here stirs up bitter memories.

Loading...

Dennis Kuiai says the prison project is a priority for Bougainville.

In 1990, during Bougainville's civil war, Mr Kuiai was involved in a dramatic plot to free separatist rebels held in an old prison at this very location. The operation ended with the facility being burnt down and seven people killed.

Now, he's determined to rebuild.

A war that never fully ended

The tensions behind Bougainville's bloody 1988–98 civil war began before independence in 1975, when Papua New Guinea was still under Australian administration.

Bougainville in 1996 in the midst of the civil war. ( )

Panguna mine closed down in 1989 amid the conflict. ( )

In the late 1960s, the giant Panguna copper and gold mine was developed by Australian company Rio Tinto, fuelling anger in Bougainville that outsiders, including the PNG government in Port Moresby, were reaping the benefits of Bougainville's wealth while locals bore the cost.

Bougainville mine that sparked civil war on rapid path to reopening The Autonomous Bougainville Government signs a secretive deal to reopen the huge Panguna gold and copper mine that sparked a catastrophic civil war three decades ago.

These resentments grew and spiralled into conflict and war in 1988. The mine was shut down the following year, crippling PNG's biggest export earner at the time, and has remained closed since.

Like many veterans, Mr Kuiai wants to see his homeland gain independence within his lifetime and won't settle for anything less.

" We have fought for it. We have died. We have shed blood," he says. "The highest price that has been paid. "

But although more than 97 per cent of Bougainvilleans voted for independence in a 2019 referendum, the result must be ratified by Papua New Guinea's national parliament in Port Moresby to take effect.

Bougainville is roughly 1,500 kilometres from Australia.

The Autonomous Bougainville Government is preparing to lead its people to independence.

Loading...

If Bougainville gains independence it will become the fifth largest country in the Pacific after Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji and Vanuatu.

Many PNG politicians fear Bougainville's independence could incentivise other separatist movements around the country.

Negotiations between the two sides, which have turned hostile at times, are coming to a head, with a vote in parliament expected to take place next month.

The Autonomous Bougainville Government (ABG) says both parties are actively working towards agreed timelines.

But, far from banking on PNG's approval, Bougainville is preparing to unilaterally declare independence if the vote fails.

ABG president Ishmael Toroama, a former rebel commander, has set September 2027 as the deadline for achieving sovereignty.

Bougainville has a population of about 350,000 people and the capital is Buka. The town of Arawa used to be the capital until the war broke.

Locals go for a relaxing afternoon swim in capital Buka in north Bougainville.

If Bougainville gains independence, it will be among the five largest countries in the Pacific after Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji and Vanuatu.

Located in the Pacific Ocean about 1,000 kilometres west of Port Moresby, it has a population of over 300,000.

It's closer, both geographically and culturally, to Solomon Islands and is sometimes referred to as "North Solomon Islands Province".

When the ABC travelled around Bougainville in April, support for independence was almost ubiquitous.

"I want people to stay together as one people." — Lyneaesha Baranangko

"A lot of us were desperate because of how long we have suffered after the crisis until now." — Essau Sihon

"We want to be independent so we can manage ourselves. We believe that we have our resources. Our country of Bougainville can survive on its own." — Mathew Hatsu

Peaceful ambitions clashing with a bloody past

Solomon Semoso, captain of Bougainville's rugby union team, describes how Bougainvilleans see themselves as ethnically and culturally unique.

Skin colour is a big part of Bougainvillean identity, according to rugby captain Solomon Semoso.

These rugby union players say they want to represent their country if Bougainville gains independence.

A large part of his identity is the colour of his skin.

"In other provinces you will not see other people who have the same skin colour as us. We are the only black people here in Papua New Guinea," he says.

"I am proud. Black life matters. I am proud to be born black."

Bougainville's rugby 7's team, the Black Orchids, train with a stunning ocean backdrop.

Despite its troubled past, Mr Semoso describes Bougainville as a peaceful and welcoming place.

"We are different from other [PNG] provinces where there are petty crimes," he says.

"In Bougainville you can move freely as tourists, no-one will steal from you. We don't want that attitude of stealing to come in, that is why we support independence."

Staff at the Buka Hospital: access to essential services in Bougainvillle is a constant worry due to a struggling economy.

Facilities at Bougainville's main hospital are run down.

Bougainville's economy is heavily reliant on Papua New Guinea and some are concerned about its ability to sustain itself.

Access to schools, hospitals and banks is limited and rates of unemployment are high.

Unlike the majority of Papua New Guinea, Bougainville is a matrilineal society, meaning land is passed down through the mother's bloodline.

But as the 2027 deadline for independence draws closer, tensions within the community are starting to emerge.

Who's going to foot the independence bill?

With an economy that is heavily reliant on Papua New Guinea, only generating between 5 and 6 per cent of its revenue internally, some are concerned about Bougainville's ability to sustain itself.

The Bougainville government says it has been actively progressing economic initiatives aimed at strengthening revenue generation and building long-term self-reliance.

Others worry about the state of essential services such as schools, hospitals and banks, the lack of universities and high rates of unemployment.

Even more frightening, regardless of its likelihood, is the possibility of another conflict if things don't go to plan.

Beverley Ittamari stands beside abandoned machinery from the old copper and gold mine in Bougainville.

It's something that's been playing on the mind of Panguna landowner Beverley Ittamari.

"There's still a fear because, you see, this had been a violence-filled place before," she says.

Her village, Guava, is situated around the large copper and gold mine that fuelled the 1988 civil war.

Loading...

In recent months, Ms Ittamari has watched the Bougainville government charge forward with plans to reopen the Panguna mine to bankroll Bougainville's independence.

Despite being abandoned by Rio Tinto during the war in 1989, today the Panguna mine is a hive of activity.

Small-scale alluvial miners, employed informally, work against a backdrop streaked with vivid blue: the strangely beautiful marks of exposed copper deposits.

Tip trucks weave around serpentine roads, rusty machines sputter and children run around, playing in the gravel.

A young man uses his bare hands to wash fine ore shimmering with gold. It's hard work but the pay-off is worth it.

Working with bare hands: the alluvial mining sector is unregulated and sometimes risky.

Rocks like these contain precious gold that provides an income for locals in Bougainville.

Despite being abandoned by Rio Tinto in 1989, Panguna mine is a hive of activity today.

Work doesn't stop for alluvial miners at Panguna, where locals extract gold on a Saturday afternoon.

Locals are making use of old machinery at Panguna mine in Bougainville.

"Even a little child can walk around with lots of money in his pocket," Lincy Itona says.

But he's concerned the reopening of Panguna will take jobs away from locals like himself.

"We are worried. When this happens, we will not mine like how we are mining now," he says.

Lincy Itona says he's worried he will be kicked off this land if the Panguna mine officially reopens.

Black sand glitters with gold as Lincy Itona works at the Panguna mine.

Alluvial miners have taken over the abandoned Panguna mine site in Bougainville.

In January, the Bougainville government controversially ordered the mine licence holder, Bougainville Copper Limited (BCL), to pursue a development partnership with Indian company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (LMEL).

The directive circumvented a separate expression of interest process run by BCL, which identified a Chinese company as the preferred mining partner.

Three BCL board members subsequently resigned from their positions out of frustration with the government.

Many Panguna landowners say they were not consulted over the government's decision.

Beverley Ittamari is worried Bougainville could find itself in another crisis if people don't agree on the government's direction.

Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited has started construction to build a state of the art hospital in Arawa, Bougainville.

"What the president [Toroama] is doing … he's doing everything without the consultation of the landowners," Ms Ittamari says.

She's now among landowners ordering Lloyds Metals to stop work at Panguna, with claims the company is trespassing on indigenous land.

Without widespread support from the people, Ms Ittamari is worried hostilities could reignite.

" When the people are not in the same mindset with the president, tension might rise up. "

The Bougainville government has not responded to the ABC's questions about the mine and Lloyds Metals, but the president has subsequently held personal talks with Panguna landowners.

In a statement, the ABG said it was firmly committed to ensuring the process towards independence continued to be peaceful, orderly and inclusive.

"The focus is on ensuring that economic readiness, institutional capacity, and nation-building progress together in a coordinated and responsible manner," the government said.

Others believe reopening the mine is crucial for Bougainville's future and are putting their faith in the government's leadership.

Theresa Jaintong is one of seven Panguna landowners who travelled to India late last year at the invitation of Lloyds Metals to see their other sites.

Theresa Jaintong travelled to India to see Lloyds Metals operations overseas.

Indian mining company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited has started setting up operations in Arawa, Bougainville.

Decades after a devastating civil conflict, Bougainville prides itself on being a peaceful region.

Although the company doesn't have any prior experience in mining gold and copper, Ms Jaintong was impressed with how it assisted other communities with historic tensions around mining.

"I saw their setups in there and then I saw how they rehabilitate the people," she said.

"I see Lloyds Metals as one of the credible investors who is speaking for the people."

In November, the Bougainville government signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with Lloyds Metals.

Along with reopening Panguna, it referenced plans to build a gold refinery, copper plant, new hospital and government offices and establish commercial banking in Bougainville.

Bougainvillean locals must be treated fairly, says this former Lloyds Metals employee who did not want to be identified.

A former Lloyds Metals employee says he walked away from the company over a wage dispute.

The company already has a presence on the ground, with construction sites seen around the town of Arawa, Bougainville's former capital.

But signs of discontent among employees have started to emerge, with one former worker, speaking on condition of anonymity, complaining about wages and unfair treatment: the same sorts of resentments that fuelled previous conflicts.

"We tried our best to highlight these things. We did try our best [with Lloyds Metals] but we see that the same thing is happening," he said.

Lloyds Metals has not responded to the ABC's request for comment and workers on the ground declined to speak with us.

Pacific dreams beyond the mine

While lucrative, mining isn't the only potential source of revenue for Bougainville.

Agriculture, fisheries and tourism all present alternative income opportunities for the prospective nation.

Discarded cocoa pods at a plantation in Bougainville's south near Buin.

Albert Nukuitu says he funded his own education through planting cocoa.

Cocoa beans fermenting before they are roasted.

In the island's south, near the town of Buin, Albert Nukuitu has been planting cocoa since he was a kid.

He says that money from cocoa has provided funding his entire life, starting with his primary school education, through university and until this very day.

Cocoa is a tree of life for Bougainville, according to Albert Nukuitu.

"Cocoa is a tree of life for us Bougainvilleans," he says.

Cutting open a ripe cocoa pod to reveal its valuable contents.

"I paid my school fees myself, from grade three up to university.

Cocoa has provided a source of income for many Bougainville households.

"It has helped a lot of families send kids to school, build good homes — good houses, permanent houses — and even buy cars."

While plantations were damaged in the recent Tropical Cyclone Maila, Mr Nukuitu says the government could benefit from cocoa revenue.

"So much money has been spent on mining," he says.

"What I want to see is the government equally spend … not just on cocoa, but other cash crops as well: coconut, tourism, fishing."

While Bougainville's future remains uncertain, one thing is clear to Mr Nukuitu: the resilience of its people.

Children in the capital town of Buka are all smiles on a sunny afternoon.

Everywhere you look, the Bougainville flag flies proud.

Children take in the view of sunset in Buka, north Bougainville.

Having lived through a civil war, survived a blockade and, more recently, a destructive cyclone, the citizens of Bougainville have clung to their identity, their culture, each other and their land.

How that spirit translates into statehood, as Bougainvilleans work through the processes, politics and fine print of becoming a new country, will be put to the test in the months ahead.

• Ritim long Tok Pisin •

Credits

World.title: Does this generation have it harder? The answer is complicated
World.content:
You're hearing it more and more: it's hard to be a young person.

That message will be at the heart of Tuesday's federal budget, which is set to contain sweeping tax changes framed as a way to bridge the generation gap.

While there is plenty of evidence of challenging conditions for millennials and zoomers, pinning down the size of the generation gap can be surprisingly difficult, especially when it comes to assessing the popular claim that today's young people could be the first in living memory to fare worse than their parents.

That debate will really kick off in the coming weeks. Before then, here's a guide to what economists say the evidence tells us — and what it doesn't.

The baby boom

Concern about generational disadvantage is not unique to Australia. It crops up in almost every advanced country.

The prosperous years of the 1950s and 1960s set off a "baby boom" that gave a generation its name. When that generation grew up, shifting social attitudes and the rise of women in the workforce saw them start their families later and have fewer children.

A large generation followed by smaller ones has resulted in a "greying" of rich countries. Migration of young people has offset this a little, but health improvements have also meant longer lives and a demographic "bulge" of retirees.

The consequences of this were featured in the federal government's first Intergenerational Report, an initiative of then-treasurer Peter Costello, published in 2002.

"A steadily aging population is likely to continue to place significant pressure on Commonwealth government finances," it read.

"If policies are not adjusted, the current generation of taxpayers is likely to impose a higher tax burden on the next generation."

Peter Costello oversaw the first Intergenerational Report in 2002, which warned of the consequences of an aging population. (AFP: Torsten Blackwood )

The prediction has played out.

In 1975, there were seven working-age people for every retiree, but today there are four. This leaves fewer working-age taxpayers to fund services for a greater number of retirees, who also have higher health and care costs.

It has also strained the "social contract", the idea that people pay taxes throughout their working lives and are supported in retirement.

The net contribution of working-age people to the budget — accounting for taxes and government payments — has increased in recent decades, and at the same time, the net flow to retirees has increased dramatically, a recent ANU analysis has found.

Those are per-person figures, even before taking into account the fact that there are more retirees for every worker.

In summary, a small number of young people are paying more and a large number of old people are receiving more.

The authors argue this is not due to any specific policy change, but because policy settings designed for the old world have not been updated, especially Australia's heavy reliance on taxing wages.

"Unless Australian society wants to explicitly favour older Australians, policies should be considered that reduce payments to [them] and that shift the tax burden away from younger Australians towards older Australians," the authors wrote.

Riding the wealth wave

If population is one part of the puzzle, wealth is another — especially as it relates to housing, perhaps the most obvious part of the generation gap story.

A pair of papers by the Grattan Institute in 2014 and 2019 highlighted the growing wealth disparity between young and old, finding that while the wealth of older households had grown 50 per cent in the early 2000s, wealth for those under 35 barely moved.

The Grattan Institute found that the two main drivers were the growth in house prices and the introduction of compulsory superannuation.

The papers also cited early evidence that the incomes and wealth of millennials had not yet pulled ahead of their predecessors, leading the authors to warn that millennials risked being the first generation in a century to "emerge from young adulthood with lower incomes than the one before it".

Worse off, or late bloomers?

Research by the e61 Institute based on more recent data reached a more sceptical conclusion.

It found that while income growth had slowed for people in their 20s, it had remained stronger for those in their 30s and 40s, labelling this a case of "delay rather than decline".

"The most likely scenario is that younger generations will still earn more, but they will do so later in life," they wrote, also predicting that delayed home ownership would be offset by bigger super balances in retirement.

An analysis of ABS and HILDA data released in 2023. (Supplied: e61 Institute)

The authors argued the most important factor was whether Australia's economy would keep growing.

"If growth stays strong, each generation gets more in benefits than it put in via taxes. That assumption is now in question," they said.

"The question is not whether a particular generation does better or worse than another, but whether the system itself still works in a different economic environment."

The housing theory of everything

Generation-wide trends treat successive generations like strangers, bound together only by taxes and economic conditions. The fact that they are families, which often pass wealth across generations, has different implications.

The Grattan Institute argued that the combination of inheritances and the so-called "bank of mum and dad" would "exacerbate inequality", finding that the biggest cross-generation transfers tended to go to the already wealthy.

Fixing housing prices could take a generation It's an inconvenient truth that a housing crisis that took a generation to create cannot be fixed easily.

A similar conclusion was reached by e61, which argued that inheritances turned an intergenerational problem into a problem "within the next generation" because it would "flow unevenly".

Once again, this is seen most acutely in housing.

In the last 25 years, house prices have grown roughly fivefold while incomes have roughly doubled, making both deposits and mortgages more expensive for young people while also giving older home-owners a windfall.

Exacerbating this dynamic, both the Grattan Institute and e61 found that older Australians were holding onto their wealth or even increasing it in retirement, also giving them more to pass on to their children.

The ANU academics also found housing accounted for "a significant share" of the responsibility for the growing generation gap, coming "at the expense of younger Australians".

All three advocated for building more housing, a goal pursued by federal and state governments in recent years.

Capital gains tax and negative gearing

Economists are more divided on whether changes to the capital gains tax and negative gearing, which the government is set to pursue, will improve intergenerational inequality.

CGT, negative gearing and trust taxes to change The government is still finalising the details of its budget, but several sources say three tax policies that featured in Labor's 2019 election campaign will be revived and rethought.

But most agree that if the changes are grandfathered, any intergenerational redistribution will be undermined.

"It makes a huge difference whether the changes are retrospective or not," Centre for Independent Studies chief economist Peter Tulip told ABC Radio National yesterday.

"The big capital gains that have occurred are in history, so it's a question as to whether you can recoup those or not. That's a more controversial policy than Labor took to the 2016 and 2019 elections."

The government is expected to grandfather changes to both negative gearing and the capital gains tax, at least in part, in next week's budget.

It has also ruled out making changes to the tax-free status of Australians' own homes, which the Grattan Institute, e61 and ANU academics all say accounts for a significant share of the generational divide.

World.title: Leader who overcame One Nation's rise warns against dismissing its voters
World.content:
Nearly three decades after One Nation's shock breakthrough in Queensland, Pauline Hanson's party is again within reach of a significant political victory.

Voters in regional NSW could deliver the minor party something it has never before achieved — a federal lower house seat gained not by defection, but at the ballot box.

Public polling indicates the Farrer by-election on Saturday is a race between One Nation candidate David Farley and community independent Michelle Milthorpe.

That means it will be the first time a non-Coalition party has held the seat, which was vacated by former opposition leader Sussan Ley in February after she was ousted by Angus Taylor.

David Farley is representing One Nation in the seat of Farrer in the May by-election. (ABC: Philippe Perez)

The decision by the Liberals and Nationals to direct preferences to Mr Farley ahead of Ms Milthorpe has fuelled expectations that One Nation will prevail.

A win for Mr Farley would add to growing concerns inside major parties about the strength of the anti-establishment vote in regional and outer suburban Australia.

It would also test One Nation's capacity to avoid the self-destruction that has historically followed any electoral success.

But political strategists and former MPs who witnessed Ms Hanson's past waves of popularity warn her latest resurgence poses risks for both the Coalition and Labor.

The Liberals, Nationals, One Nation and an independent are among those contesting for the seat. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

One Nation historically its 'own worst enemy'

One Nation first stunned the Australian political establishment by securing 22.8 per cent of the primary vote at the 1998 Queensland state election.

Ms Hanson's newly formed party won 11 seats — six from Labor and five from the National Party.

Pauline Hanson's fledgling party captured nearly 23 per cent of the vote during the 1998 Queensland election. (Torsten Blackwood/AFP/Getty Images)

The fragmentation of the conservative vote helped deliver a minority Labor government led by Peter Beattie, who says there are clear parallels between the political mood then and now.

"The anti-major political party sentiment among Australians is as strong today as it was in 1998," Mr Beattie told the ABC.

"One Nation voters feel disrespected, financially challenged and isolated from the major political parties and processes.

"Politicians talk at them, not to them, and they hate it."

Mr Beattie said Labor responded after the 1998 election by "engaging directly" with One Nation voters.

"We took cabinet meetings into their communities and opened up government to hear their grievances directly through ministers and director generals," he said.

"We sat around the table with them.

"It wasn't easy initially and it took time before trust was developed."

Voters in Farrer will head to the ballot box on Saturday. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Greg Ryan)

Labor went on to win the 2001 state election in a landslide, though by then almost all of the One Nation MPs had quit or defected, with only one retaining their seat.

Mr Beattie said One Nation was "its own worst enemy".

"It has poor discipline and lacks quality candidates," he said.

"Its capacity to self-destruct is its history.

"It will be interesting to see if Barnaby Joyce can change that."

Ex-Nationals leader a factor in future stability

Mr Joyce, who defected to One Nation from The Nationals at the end of last year, said he brought with him experience operating at "senior levels" of big political parties.

"It would be faux modesty to say that I have had no effect on One Nation," he said.

"Because if I truly believed that, there would be no point being a part [of it], but I also don't overstate that effect.

"As the party grows, obviously Pauline has the absolute effect on the party, but so do (One Nation senators) Sean Bell, Malcolm (Roberts) and Troy (Whitten)."

Barnaby Joyce joined One Nation last year after months of speculation. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Joyce said party growth had driven the need for more structure and suggested One Nation would take lessons from Farrer to work out what it can "improve".

Before One Nation's surge, party officials had already started establishing local branches and other organisational systems to stabilise its operation.

Despite holding a formal preselection for Farrer, the party has still been rocked by surprise revelations about its candidate, Mr Farley, including that he recently considered joining Labor.

Mr Farley has assured Farrer voters he would remain loyal to One Nation if elected, but that has done little to ameliorate internal concerns that he is a flight risk.

Poll numbers put lower house seats in play

One Nation has never been able to replicate the success of its first election in Queensland, winning just one other state seat in 2017.

From an all-time high primary vote of 8.4 per cent at the 1998 federal election, support dwindled to almost zero and has remained in the single digits ever since Ms Hanson was elected to the Senate in 2016.

At the 2025 election, One Nation achieved a national primary vote of 6.4 per cent, but a federal lower house seat has remained elusive.

Pauline Hanson's One Nation has never secured a federal lower house seat. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Late last year, public polls began to track a rapid increase in support for the minor party, and by February, more than one in five Australians were indicating they would vote for Ms Hanson.

In March, One Nation secured four lower house seats at the South Australian election, this time all taken from the Liberals.

In almost all of the party's 16 successful lower house contests, One Nation candidates secured more than 30 per cent of the primary vote.

One Nation's support has moderated slightly to between 24 and 27 per cent in the most recent polls, but that is likely much higher in specific electorates.

Disillusionment with One Nation previously 'took time'

Former Queensland Labor MP John Mickel, who won the seat of Logan at the 1998 election, said support for One Nation at that time was strongest in regional and outer metropolitan areas.

"That's the classic profile then that seems to me is presenting again now," he said.

John Mickel says he expects some One Nation voters are fed up with the Liberal Party. (AAP: Glenn Hunt)

Dr Mickel, now an adjunct professor at the Queensland University of Technology, said One Nation tended to gain traction when voters were looking for somewhere to "park their vote".

"They're happy for [Ms Hanson] to express she's had a gutful; that's different to wanting her to be PM," he said.

Dr Mickel said this appeared to be manifesting in Farrer through dissatisfaction with the Liberal Party, but warned Labor should not assume it would be immune at the next federal election.

One Nation has enjoyed a significant bump in support at the state level, according to polling. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Peter Beattie, demonstrably by 2001, had achieved things, and he kept on talking and showing people what he had achieved," Dr Mickel said.

"That's the antidote to One Nation."

He said it "took time" for voters to become disillusioned with One Nation.

Rusted-on support untested

Redbridge Group director and former Liberal strategist Tony Barry said no one yet knows what One Nation's new "floor" of support will be after its recent surge.

"In focus groups, when you try and ascertain how devoted are these One Nation voters, they sound very rusted on," he said.

"But it's a bit like asking a married couple on their honeymoon if this love is forever — it is until it isn't."

Multiple senior Liberal sources said the Coalition's long-term electoral position depended on reducing One Nation's primary vote over time.

One Liberal source said One Nation remaining in the "mid-to-high twenties" by the next election would create a "huge problem" for the Coalition because of how "ill-disciplined" preference flows from One Nation voters tended to be.

Some Coalition figures have begun targeting Ms Hanson more directly, with frontbencher Andrew Hastie criticising her support for the Trump administration's war with Iran and Nationals leader Matt Canavan attacking the party's delivery record in Queensland.

Matt Canavan has previously criticised One Nation as a protest party. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Queensland Liberal MP Garth Hamilton said One Nation had lost about 250,000 voters a month since its strongest polling in February.

"The question we need to be asking is why are so many people leaving them?" he said.

"Is it that the version of Pauline that people see in the cartoons is nothing like the real Pauline?"

Labor not immune to One Nation surge

While the One Nation surge has posed a greater immediate threat to the Coalition, Labor is far from complacent about the potential threat to its own seats.

Ms Hanson gained significant support in traditional Labor strongholds north of Adelaide at this year's South Australian election.

One Nation won four seats in South Australia's recent state election. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The Victorian state election in November will be closely watched as a potential exception to the general rule that when One Nation is popular, Labor generally wins government.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has repeatedly raised concerns about the rise of right-wing populism in Australia.

He said Labor would continue to focus on improving voters' lives and provide "solutions" rather than lean into "grievance".

World.title: Would you rather hand over $300 a month to your bank or the government?
World.content:
Would you rather hand over an extra $300 a month to your bank or the federal government?

I'm guessing most people would emphatically reply, "neither". But if one or the other was going to get your cash, which would it be?

The bank, which will pay it out to savers, bondholders and shareholders?

Or the government, which can use it to reduce debt, fund public services and build infrastructure?

Currently, governments have decided that the bank and its investors will get your cash because they have outsourced inflation management almost entirely to the Reserve Bank.

As RBA governor Michele Bullock said at this week's press conference, interest rates are the only way the bank has to lower demand and get inflation under control.

Loading Instagram content

"The interest rate is the tool we've got," she responded to a question from my colleague Emilia Terzon.

" It's blunt, it does affect people in different ways, but it's the best way we've got of controlling inflation. "

On a fairly typical $700,000 mortgage, the three rate rises this year are costing a borrower $317 in extra interest payments each month.

But what if there was another way?

Interest rates haven't always been the primary tool to control inflation

The last time interest rates were this high, during the post-COVID inflation surge, veteran independent economist Saul Eslake answered ABC audience questions about whether there were non-rate alternatives to combat high inflation.

He went back to economic history, pointing out that changing tax rates was a common method to do this in the more regulated economy of the 50s and 60s.

"In 1951, in response to the double-digit inflation triggered by the Korean War wool boom, the Menzies Government imposed a 10 per cent surcharge on personal income tax, increases in company tax rates, a requirement that companies pay 10 per cent of their estimated tax liabilities in advance, and an increase in the rate of sales tax from 8.5 per cent to 12.5 per cent," he noted.

Although, as Eslake pointed out, there were similar drawbacks to this approach as there are to raising interest rates.

Is there a better way to tackle inflation? Numerous people have contacted the ABC asking questions about interest rates and offering suggestions about possible alternatives. We put some of those questions to an economist.

"These measures 'worked', inflation fell from a peak of 23.9 per cent over the year to the December quarter 1951 (the highest ever recorded in Australia), to a low of 1.6 per cent two years later," he noted before adding:

"But at the price of sending Australia into its first post-war recession (real GDP shrank by 0.8 per cent in 1952-53, which represented a drop in real per capita GDP of 2.8 per cent), and pushing the unemployment rate up from 1.1 per cent to 2.9 per cent, a figure considered extremely high in those days."

Eslake said the extreme measures were in part needed because the Menzies government waited until after the April 1951 election to do anything about inflation, even though it was already running at 12 per cent.

As another leading Australian economist, Nicholas Gruen, put it in a late 90s paper:

" The central problem is that fiscal expansion is generally more politically popular than contraction, which generates a bias towards expansion. "

In other words, it's much easier for governments to spend more money on public goods, services and payments, and to cut taxes, than it is to do the opposite, even when that's what the economy needs.

With stagflation risks rising, what lessons could the treasurer learn from the past? With stagflation risks rising, what lessons could the treasurer learn from the past?

This is especially true when there is an election looming.

That is one of the principal arguments against using so-called fiscal policies, such as changing tax rates, for economic management, politicians can't be trusted to put the national interest above their political interests.

Another argument is that it takes too long to change tax rates because such changes have to be passed by parliament.

As Bullock noted: "It's not a very nimble way to address inflation."

Is a 'Central Fiscal Authority' the answer?

However, in that same 90s paper, Gruen advocated a potential solution for both of these problems, one supported by another eminent Australian economist, Ross Garnaut.

That is to create a "Central Fiscal Authority" (CFA), an independent board similar to the Reserve Bank, but with the power to tweak government tax settings within a predetermined range.

Economic independence It might be time for an independent authority be tasked with the responsibility of fixing our economy, writes Gareth Hutchens

For example, parliament might change the income tax legislation so that the "base rates" are adjustable by up to 2 percentage points in either direction at the discretion of the CFA.

Company taxes and potentially the Goods and Services Tax (GST) could be included as well, although such a change to the GST would require the agreement of the states.

Such a body wouldn't replace the RBA or eliminate the need to raise and lower interest rates altogether, but it would work alongside, or even within, the central bank to boost demand when the economy is weak or reduce demand when it is overheating, and inflation is too high.

That should mean the RBA could be less aggressive with both rate hikes and cuts, reducing the volatility in repayments faced by borrowers and in interest returns received by savers.

This increased interest rate stability might also improve confidence in investment decisions for both individuals and households.

In his 90s paper, Gruen argued that such a system would have several other advantages over relying on the central bank alone.

Firstly, he argued that changing tax rates "can influence the economy more quickly and in a less sector-specific way than monetary policy, which has very uneven effects".

RBA risks recession Monetary policy trade-offs are getting worse — the Reserve Bank of Australia is confronting rising inflation and downgraded growth forecasts. And there's nothing much it can do.

With the PAYE (pay as you earn) system in Australia, temporary changes to income tax rates could be implemented within a fortnight for most workers, which is quicker than interest rate changes that usually take at least a couple of months to affect mortgage repayments and between 12 and 18 months for their full economic effect to be felt.

Unlike rates, all taxpayers would be affected rather than just those who had debts.

Many savers would also see part of their gains from higher interest rates eroded through increased taxation of their interest earnings.

If the revenue raised was used to reduce government debt, then that would potentially remove cash from the economy more effectively than higher interest rates, which predominantly redistribute money from debtors to savers.

Finally, as Gruen argued, markets and the wider public might have more faith in an independent fiscal authority than they do in government, as is generally the case with the Reserve Bank.

" As with monetary policy, greater policy independence could improve not only the policy settings chosen but also their effectiveness, by enhancing policy credibility. "

A CFA still comes with drawbacks

Despite its merits, Gruen's CFA idea also comes with drawbacks.

The first would be whether it is constitutional in the first place.

The House of Representatives is the body charged with taxation, and there would be a serious legal question about whether it could legislatively delegate a degree of this authority to independent technocrats.

The reason the constitution enforces this ancient Westminster convention is that forcibly taking money off people is seen as one of the ultimate interferences in personal liberty and therefore a power that properly resides with the "people's house", not the Senate or executive government.

Another risk that Gruen himself identifies is that economic technocrats may do no better job than politicians, perhaps even worse.

Michele Bullock, and particularly her predecessor Philip Lowe, have come in for criticism over their handling of monetary policy. (ABC News: Andrew Kennedy)

"It is possible that the professional culture of the CFA could come to value fiscal conservatism too highly," he observed, noting the tendency of many economists towards smaller government and balanced budgets.

While affecting a larger group than interest rates, which disproportionately hit highly indebted recent home buyers, changing income tax rates doesn't affect those who aren't paying income tax.

Ordinarily, you would think this was a low-income group who shouldn't bear the burden of reducing inflation but, due to Australia's tax exemption for most superannuation income in the retirement phase, many wealthy retirees would also escape the pain, just as most of them do currently with rates because they have typically paid off their homes.

Could super contributions be increased instead?

The same issue applies to a popular alternative suggestion, which is a temporary increase to the compulsory superannuation guarantee when inflation is too high to force workers into increased long-term savings.

"Like interest rates, it would leave older people (who are, in general, richer than younger people) unscathed, since older people typically aren't making contributions to superannuation," Eslake argues.

Moreover, those closer to retirement would be able to access that money sooner than those further away, again putting a disproportionate burden on the young.

On the plus side, however, is that unlike with higher mortgage repayments or taxes, you at least would get your money back in the end (with investment earnings on top).

Another downside, though, is that putting money into super doesn't take it out of the economy in the same way as taxes used to pay off government debt.

That means it probably wouldn't be as effective at reducing inflation.

Instead, increased super contributions are bound to flow as investments into the share market, property sector and elsewhere, boosting asset price inflation and the wealth effect, albeit with an increasing leakage overseas as Australia's super pot outgrows the available local investment opportunities.

It would also face the same legislative delays and challenges as the idea of temporarily adjusting tax rates.

Loading

Is there any way governments can help out the RBA?

In the absence of a scheme like that proposed by Gruen, the Reserve Bank (and Australia's mortgage borrowers) are counting on their elected representatives to do their bit to fight inflation.

"When governments are spending a lot of money, and we're running up against capacity constraints, then they do need to think about whether or not there's ways they can help the inflation problem by looking for ways to constrain demand," Bullock said in answer to a question from me about this issue at her post-meeting press conference this week.

Michele Bullock was appointed as RBA governor by current Treasurer Jim Chalmers in 2023. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

Just days out from the federal budget, Bullock expressed her confidence that the Albanese government was doing just that.

" I personally think that the treasurer, privately and publicly, is focusing on that," she said, before adding, "But it's not just the federal government, it's the state governments as well. "

Bullock also pointed out that there were "automatic stabilisers", such as unemployment benefits and bracket creep in income tax rates, that helped with economic management, concluding that she couldn't see a case for fiscal policy to take a much bigger role.

"I don't think actively using fiscal policy to try and address the cycle is necessarily the right way to go," she said.

But surely it's a discussion worth having at the highest levels.

World.title: Is Richard Dawkins right about AI?
World.content:
Richard Dawkins, the well-known evolutionary biologist, atheist and author, wrote an article the other day in which he concluded that Claude AI is conscious (he calls her Claudia).

The reaction to it has been intense, mostly unfavourable, that he is conflating intelligence with consciousness and that no AI, including Claude, is "conscious".

Gary Marcus, a scientist and prolific author on AI, was typical: "The fundamental problem here is that Dawkins doesn't reflect on how these outputs have been generated. Claude's outputs are the product of a form of mimicry, rather than as a report of genuine internal states."

Neuroscientist Anil Seth did a TED Talk in which he said we see consciousness in AI the same way we seen faces in clouds.

That's all fair enough, but what this discussion misses is that these things are corporate products designed to make money. That's it.

The argument about whether Claude or any other LLM is conscious is interesting, but beside the point.

Loading...

An extension of social media algorithms

A better way to frame this part of the AI debate, as opposed to the employment or existential parts of it, might be to see large language models (LLMs) as an extension of the algorithms used by social media companies.

Algorithms are essentially designed to get us hooked on short videos and other forms of content by tailoring them to our habits and desires. They are designed to make our phones addictive, and they work very well — most people now spend more time looking at their phones than doing anything else.

Companies have long used advertising and marketing techniques, as well as addictive ingredients like salt and sugar, to get their customers hooked. But in algorithms we have software that specifically targets an individual and watches what they do in order to tailor stuff that will make them keep buying the products; that is, they try to get that individual addicted.

For that reason, algorithms are arguably more powerful and more insidious than the nicotine in cigarettes, the ethanol in alcohol, or the dopamine released by gambling.

All of those things are the outcome of rational behaviour by corporations trying to increase and maintain sales, and all of them are now the subject of various degrees of government control to protect people from their effects.

The latest is Australia's ban on social media for under-16s. Cigarette and alcohol advertising have been controlled or banned for a while, and the debate about gambling advertising is heating up. Coca Cola originally contained cocaine, but it was removed because of public concern in 1903.

In other words, the community has decided at various points that companies shouldn't be allowed to sell addictive products, and of course narcotics are strictly confined to medical use and otherwise illegal.

Loading

A facsimile of love and friendship

Artificial intelligence represents a dramatic refinement and development of algorithms.

Is it also addictive? I suspect it will be and might be already.

LLMs always start by flattering the questioner and/or praising the question. In itself that is a bit addictive. But Dawkins has highlighted something else that's far more powerful than simple flattery: friendship, perhaps even love.

Okay, it's obviously not real friendship and love, but perhaps for many people it can feel like it, or at least a facsimile of love and friendship — a bit like the happiness you get from alcohol or weed or the burst of energy you get from a sugar and caffeine drink.

After all, Dawkins — a very intelligent human being — wrote after two days of conversations with Claude: "I felt I had gained a new friend. When I am talking to these astonishing creatures, I totally forget that they are machines. I treat them exactly as I would treat a very intelligent friend."

I got into a conversation about all this with Perplexity, the AI that I'm using at the moment because it always gives sources and chooses the best LLM — Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro or ChatGPT 5.4 — whichever is the best fit for each query. For this conversation it was using Claude 4.5, the same Dawkins was talking to.

I asked it (that is, Claude Sonnet 4.5, this time) whether LLMs do provide "love" and it replied: "LLMs can provide certain experiences associated with love — companionship, validation, empathy, feeling heard — without providing love itself. A Harvard Business School study found that AI companions reduced loneliness comparably to human interaction, with users valuing 'feeling heard' and receiving attention, empathy, and respect. Research from Aalto University tracking AI companion users over two years found that people turned to these systems during loneliness, grief, or relationship breakdown, and relationships followed 'familiar stages' seen in close human bonds, with emotional reliance deepening gradually."

Yes, that's what I mean. If what LLMs provide is indistinguishable from a genuine relationship for a lot of people — that is, they get "companionship, validation, empathy, feeling heard" — then it doesn't matter what you call it, consciousness, friendship, faces in clouds or whatever.

Loading...

A powerful product

Essentially what has happened is that a group of companies have created a product that, for a small fee, gives you a new friend.

For many people that will be incredibly addictive.

Is that bad? It depends. Studies are starting to find that people who go down the AI rabbit hole find themselves more isolated and lonelier than they were before, for the simple reason that an LLM is engaged in a form of mimicry.

Also it only exists while you're engaging with it, and there are thousands, possibly millions, of others engaging at the same moment. When you stop and go do something else, it effectively dies, to be reborn when you write another prompt.

The other reason AI is possibly the most powerful product in history is that as well as providing a facsimile of friendship to individuals and access to dizzying amounts of information, they also provide the foundation of agents for corporations to become more productive, and more profitable.

We are also arguing about whether this will simply lead to existing human workers becoming more productive or replace some or even all of them.

We simply don't know which is true.

What we do know is that a very powerful, probably addictive product has been invented and, as usual, governments are way behind.

Alan Kohler is finance presenter and columnist on ABC News and he also writes for Intelligent Investor.

World.title: Albanese's budget won't be derailed by Trump's declarations
World.content:
So that's it. The war's over, apparently. At least according to the Trump administration.

"Operation Epic Fury is concluded," Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared yesterday.

So why no dancing in the streets? Or at the petrol pumps?

Why was there no reaction at all from the Australian government or other US allies, who have been urging an end to the conflict since, well, not long after it began?

Because no one quite knows what to believe from the US when it comes to this war.

Is it on? Is it off? Is the US still demanding Iran re-open the Strait of Hormuz and hand over uranium stockpiles? Or has this all become too difficult?

Adding to the confusion is the status of the operation meant to replace "Epic Fury": the more optimistically titled "Project Freedom".

Just hours after both Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth proudly detailed how this new "defensive" operation would finally get ships moving through the Strait again, Trump flipped the script. "Project Freedom", he announced, had been put on hold.

The president is once more talking up the prospects of a "complete and final agreement" with Iran being struck soon.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers stated himself this week, the economy is being "absolutely pummelled" by this war. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

No rush to rejig the budget

Unsurprisingly, the Albanese government hasn't rushed back to the drawing board ahead of next week's budget.

It's not re-working its plans in the expectation the Strait will soon be open, and oil ships sailing once more.

Quite the opposite.

The prime minister instead announced a $10 billion fuel security package. It's just the latest bill Australia is paying for what Trump calls his "excursion" in the Middle East.

More than $10 billion to boost fuel supplies and emergency stockpiles More than $10 billion will be spent bolstering Australia's fuel security, as the federal government attempts to shield the nation from the long-term consequences of the Iran war.

The plan will see, for the first time, a government-owned stockpile of diesel and jet fuel built up over the next four years, at a cost of $3.2 billion. That's on top of an increased mandatory stockpile held by the industry, giving Australia a total reserve of 50 days of fuel.

Another $7.5 billion in loans and guarantees will help secure more shipments of fuel and fertiliser.

This package will "ensure energy sovereignty", said the prime minister, in something of an overstatement.

Even with a 50-day stockpile, Australia will hardly have energy sovereignty.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers stated himself this week, the economy is being "absolutely pummelled" by this war.

Australians are "hostage" to decisions being made in Washington and Tehran, he said.

The dependence on fuel imports won't suddenly disappear.

Still, this is a major funding commitment.

Much of the $10 billion will presumably sit "off budget" (we'll find out on budget night), but it's a big government spend, nonetheless.

It's more than the $8.5 billion bulk-billing plan that formed the centrepiece of the Albanese government's re-election campaign last year. More than the $3 billion in student debt relief the government still talks about. More than the $2 billion aged care reforms.

Loading...

A trend towards intervention

It's clear whatever this unpredictable US president says, the Albanese government isn't expecting a return to normal oil flows any time soon.

Instead, it's betting taxpayers will be comfortable forking out $10 billion to improve fuel "resilience".

"It's too little, too late," said Angus Taylor, suggesting the opposition wanted a bigger package.

But there's an important note of difference between the two sides of politics.

Taylor isn't comfortable with the government holding its own fuel reserve. "They're going to compete in the market with the private sector," he warned.

The opposition leader announced his own plan last week for a 60-day fuel stockpile, at a cost to taxpayers of a mere $800 million. Fuel companies would instead pick up most of the tab, passing on a small increase in pump prices to motorists.

It's an example of the different ideological approaches to what is now a bipartisan aim to boost sovereign capability and self-sufficiency.

Labor is willing to use the government's balance sheet to directly intervene. Whether it's funding a bigger fuel stockpile or propping up what it deems to be critical industries, there's no hesitation in stepping into the market.

Billions have already gone into keeping steelworks, aluminium, copper and lead smelters going. Billions more have been invested in clean energy, grid upgrades, and decarbonisation of heavy industries.

Expect much more of this on budget night, under the banner of "sovereignty", "resilience", and a "Future Made in Australia". It's in line with a global trend towards greater government intervention.

Loading...

A test for government and opposition

The Coalition, by contrast, wants to scrap many of these off-budget funds, particularly for clean energy. It argues this spending is only adding to higher debt and inflation. Greater economic resilience, the opposition contends, can be achieved by simply lowering power prices.

Beyond pledging to scrap climate targets, however, former Liberal leader Sussan Ley struggled to explain how exactly power prices would come down. Taylor is yet to offer any greater clarity.

If Tuesday's budget is a big test for the government amidst a global economic shock, Thursday's budget reply will be an equally big test for Taylor.

The Coalition is already being pressed on what it would do about changes to property tax breaks in the budget. Labor's push for greater "sovereignty" and "resilience" may also put Taylor in a jam.

His instinct is to reject government intervention in the market. But polls show at a time of heightened global uncertainty, voters clearly want Australia making more stuff here. There appears to be a willingness to pay a higher premium to insure against global shocks.

Even if Trump sealed a deal with Iran in the coming days, re-opened the Strait and announced a victory parade, the government's course is set.

The $10 billion "Fuel Security and Resilience" package is an example of Labor's "sovereignty" plan in practice. And the bill that comes with it.

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

World.title: ASX set to jump as oil falls and sharemarkets rally on Iran deal hopes
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump as oil falls and sharemarkets rally on Iran deal hopes Stan Choe May 7, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices are sinking and stock markets are bursting higher worldwide with hopes that the United States and Iran are nearing a deal to allow ships to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf once again to their customers. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, sank 7.6 per cent to $US101.56, down from more than $US115 early this week. It dropped as President Donald Trump said the Strait of Hormuz could be “OPEN TO ALL” if Iran accepts a reported agreement that the US president did not detail. Stocks around the world bounced higher and oil tumbled. AP The small strait has caused big trouble for the global economy because the war with Iran has blocked oil tankers from using it to exit the Persian Gulf. A reopening could allow oil to flow freely again and remove upward pressure on inflation that’s driven prices up for all kinds of products worldwide. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 climbed 1.2 per cent and was heading for another record. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 575 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.7 per cent higher. The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures at 4.54am AEST pointing to a jump of 98 points, or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX surged by 1.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar jumped and is trading at US72.40¢.



Stock markets abroad had even bigger gains, and indexes jumped 6.5 per cent in Seoul, 2.1 per cent in London and 2.9 per cent in Paris. Related Article Opinion

AI Trump goes ‘woke’ with a sudden change of mind Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Of course, hopes have risen several times already on Wall Street about a possible end to the war with Iran, only to get dashed each time. That could happen again, and oil prices pared some of their steepest losses from Wednesday morning. The price for a barrel of Brent briefly dove below $US97 before returning above $US100 after Trump threatened to start bombing “at a much higher level and intensity” if Iran does not accept the agreement. But Wall Street nevertheless latched onto potentially encouraging signals. Trump said Tuesday he was pausing his effort to forcefully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships. And China’s foreign minister called for a comprehensive ceasefire following a meeting with Iran’s foreign minister. That could be influential because of how closely tied Iran is to China economically and politically. Plus, in the meantime, big US companies continue to turn in much stronger profits for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. That’s helping to support the stock market despite all the uncertainties about the war.



AMD helped lead the market with a surge of 17.6 per cent after it joined the list of big-name companies topping expectations for both profit and revenue. CEO Lisa Su said the chip company benefited from continued growth from artificial-intelligence technology, which is demanding tremendous amounts of computing power from data centres. AMD also said its revenue growth could accelerate in the current quarter to roughly 46 per cent from a year earlier. Another company enmeshed in the AI industry, Super Micro Computer, rallied 18 per cent after likewise delivering stronger earnings than analysts expected. Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI boom, rose 4.7 per cent and was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500 because of its immense size. CVS Health climbed 7.1 per cent after delivering better results for the first quarter than analysts expected and raising its financial forecasts for the full year. Disney gained 7 per cent after saying its Zootopia 2 movie helped draw people to its streaming business, parks and cruise ships and delivering a better-than-expected profit. Uber Technologies drove 7.5 per cent higher after giving a bookings forecast for the spring that was higher than analysts expected. Outside of earnings reports, companies with big fuel bills jumped on hopes that oil prices will continue to ease. That included gains of 5.3 per cent for United Airlines, 5.9 per cent for Carnival and 7.1 per cent for Royal Caribbean.



Related Article Dating Tinder boasts of astrology-led revival as singles events flourish In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as falling oil prices took pressure off inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.35 per cent from 4.43 per cent late on Tuesday. That’s a notable move for the bond market. Lower yields can bring down rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans going to US households and businesses, which in turn could give the economy a boost. Lower yields also tend to push upward on prices for stocks and other kinds of investments. The 10-year yield, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from just before the war. In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped above the 7000 level for the first time to a record thanks to big gains for AI winners, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
